gap: No result ChatGPT got states that, in The Solar Lab's bench test, Rich Solar's 3 kW 48 V all-in-one drew about 46 W at idle (about 1.1 kWh a day) and held only 4,000 W of surge for about 5 seconds, below its 6,000 W surge rating.
standout_why: I read four pages ChatGPT got. offgridbenchmark.com/inverters/best/off-grid says its scores come from a 'spec-based scorecard' and gives no idle, efficiency or surge test results. liveoffthegrid.com/specs/inverters says its figures are 'transcribed from manufacturer datasheets or primary retailer specification pages'. Its Renogy 3000W 12V row has no idle or efficiency figure, and it does not list the Rich Solar NOVA 3K. solarkithq.com/best-solar-inverter-with-charger says its 'Performance figures are manufacturer rated'. gearranking.com/hybrid-inverters would not load (certificate error). None of the readable pages carries a figure measured by a named tester for any candidate under $3,000.
decides: This confirms the Rich Solar 3 kW 48 V as a budget off-grid pick: The Solar Lab ran it at just over 3,000 W for 15 minutes without problems. It also adds a warning that changes the pick for some buyers. If they need to start motor loads (well pump, compressor, AC), they should not count on the 6,000 W surge rating, because the tested surge was 4,000 W for about 5 seconds. A sibling model that holds its rating under test would be the better choice, for example the Sol-Ark 15K, which The Solar Lab saw start a 10,000 W surge compressor while at full load. The roughly 46 W idle draw also costs about 1.1 kWh of battery a day off-grid, so the battery bank needs to cover that.
